body.heading: The invitation to play
paragraphs: Watch two dogs meet. One drops its front legs, raises its rear, tail wagging: the play bow. It is a promise that what follows — the chasing, wrestling and mock-biting — is not a fight. Animals that play have signals like this to say: this is the game version, not the real one.
Stronger or older animals often handicap themselves, biting softly or letting a youngster win a tumble. Play only works if both sides keep it play, and animals police that boundary carefully.

body.heading: Sliding, surfing and showing off
paragraphs: Ravens and crows have been watched sliding down snowy roofs and muddy banks, climbing back up, and sliding again — no food, no destination, just the slide. Dolphins ride the bow waves of boats and surf shore waves, and carry pieces of seaweed to one another in what looks very much like a passing game.

New Zealand's kea parrots even have a special play call: hearing it puts other kea in a playful mood, a kind of contagious laughter. Scientists who study animal play take it seriously because it is costly — energy spent on fun must be buying something important, like practice, bonding or learning.

body.heading: Try it: be a play detective
paragraphs: Watch a pet or animals in a park for ten minutes with a notebook. Note the moment play starts: what signal invited it? Note how the animals keep it friendly, and what happens when one has had enough.

Then ask the harder question scientists ask: how can you tell play from real chasing or fighting? The bow, the relaxed faces, the taking of turns — once you can spot the signals, you will see play everywhere.

takeaway: From a dog's bow to a raven's snow slide, play is one of nature's oldest inventions — practice and friendship in the same gesture.
